# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Reaction performance likely depends categorically on catalyst and solvent, with a finite temperature/time optimum; anonymous indices carry no ordinal meaning. A first-pass screen should vary categories and thermal severity. A reaction-phase HPLC reading should identify whether poor final recovery originates before or after workup.

## H2 [tentative]
The nominal dossier predicts X0 has the strongest product/impurity partition selectivity (~3.30) and the greatest single-contact product transfer among listed extractants under its stated conditions, but only ~35% product transfer at the anchor phase ratio. Thus X0 is the initial extraction choice; repeated contacts or higher organic ratio should raise recovery. This expectation will be revised if observed assays contradict the dossier.

## Decision rule
Prioritize final purity >=0.80, then recovery. Use early batches as a categorical reaction screen with consistent X0 workup; use later batches to test extraction intensity and repeat the best process. Numerical differences smaller than declared assay noise will not be treated alone as evidence of effects.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in screened scope]
Catalyst C1 is preferred for further work. The direct final assay for C1/S0 at 380 K, 3600 s gave purity ~0.618 and recovery ~0.187 (event runner-operation-0026), whereas C2/S0 and C3/S0 at the harsher 400 K, 7200 s produced lower purity (~0.339 and ~0.470; events runner-operation-0033 and -0040). Because temperature/time are confounded with catalyst in these comparisons, the categorical catalyst ranking is provisional outside the screened conditions.

## H2 [supported for C1 at 380 K, 3600 s]
Among solvents, S3 gave the highest direct recovery (~0.300) with similar purity (~0.645; event runner-operation-0061), versus S0/S1/S2 recoveries ~0.187/0.241/0.250 (events runner-operation-0026, -0047, -0054). These differences exceed the declared assay recovery noise for S3 versus S0 and suggest a real solvent effect; S3 is selected for optimization.

## H3 [revised]
The initial X0 extraction attempt did not meet specification: purity ~0.768 and reported recovery 0 after an extraction/wash/concentration train (event runner-operation-0019). The zero recovery may reflect selection or concentration losses, not solely partitioning. Future workup tests should avoid unnecessary concentration and compare an organic isolate directly.

## Next tests
With C1/S3, vary thermal duration/temperature, then apply X0 extraction to the best reaction. Purity >=0.80 remains the gate; among qualifying batches maximize recovery. A repeat of the selected process is needed if resources permit.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in screened scope]
Catalyst C1 with solvent S3 is the best reaction combination tested. Extending C1/S3 from 3600 s to 7200 s at 380 K increased final recovery from ~0.300 (event runner-operation-0061) to ~0.412 (event runner-operation-0075), while purity remained about 0.61–0.65. Batch-to-batch reaction HPLC readings for this longer process were broadly consistent (~0.392–0.396 recovery in events runner-operation-0080, -0098, and -0115), supporting repeatability of the upstream trend despite assay noise.

## H2 [rejected as implemented]
The nominal X0 selectivity did not translate to a qualifying workup. The correctly contacted X0 organic isolate in the final batch gave purity ~0.539 and recovery ~0.088 (event runner-operation-0124), worse than the direct reaction isolate. Earlier workups also suffered procedural failures: excessive post-separation drying or an omitted extractant addition left zero-recovery samples (events runner-operation-0093 and -0110). These failures show that phase-operation validation and retained-volume checks are essential; they do not establish that all X0 processes are intrinsically ineffective.

## H3 [unresolved]
No completed batch met the required purity >=0.80. Batch 1 approached it (~0.768) but had reported recovery 0 after wash/concentration (event runner-operation-0019). Thus the available evidence does not support a gate-compliant process. A future test should use the C1/S3 reaction, smaller reaction-solvent charge or a separate transfer vessel to permit a high organic:aqueous ratio, and assay the organic phase before drying; a gentle wash could then be evaluated separately.

## Final decision
Recommend completed batch 9 (C1/S3, 380 K, 7200 s, direct isolate) because it has the highest observed recovery (~0.412; event runner-operation-0075) and the best native score among completed batches, with low mass-balance error. This is explicitly a best-available, noncompliant recommendation: purity ~0.612 is below 0.80. The decision would change in favor of any reproducible completed process attaining >=0.80 purity with nonzero recovery.

payload.report:
## 1. Overall interpretation

This world is best explained as a coupled reaction–partition–handling system. A limiting reagent is converted in parallel to a desired product and unwanted material; catalyst, solvent, temperature, and residence time alter both productive and unproductive pathways. Purification then changes the composition and recovery of the selected phase through liquid–liquid partitioning and through potentially severe handling losses. Measurements made before and after purification do not necessarily describe the same material, so a high final-assay “conversion” after extraction cannot be interpreted as high reactor conversion.

No completed batch satisfied the required purity of 0.80. Batch 9 was therefore sealed as the best available, explicitly noncompliant recommendation because it had the highest observed recovery, about 0.412, and the best diagnostic score, while its purity was only about 0.612.

## 2. Proposed reaction mechanism

A minimal phenomenological network is

R → P  (desired product)
R → I  (competitive impurity/byproduct)
P → D  (secondary degradation)

with effective rates that depend on the categorical catalyst C, solvent S, and temperature T. One possible model is

dR/dt = −(kP(C,S,T)+kI(C,S,T))R,
dP/dt = kP(C,S,T)R − kD(C,S,T)P,
dI/dt = kI(C,S,T)R,

where each rate could have an Arrhenius-like temperature dependence. This is a useful explanatory model, not an identified kinetic law: the campaign did not contain time series sufficient to fit individual rate constants.

The observations suggest that increasing thermal severity generally accelerates desired formation, but also increases byproduct formation and does not materially improve product purity. Thus conversion alone is not the objective; productive and impurity pathways accelerate together.

## 3. Catalyst effects

Batches 2–4 supplied the main catalyst evidence in solvent S0, although their thermal conditions were not identical.

- Batch 2, C1/S0 at 380 K for 3600 s, gave a direct final conversion of 0.304, purity 0.618, recovery 0.187, yield 0.187, and byproduct signal 0.099.
- Batch 3, C2/S0 at 400 K for 7200 s, gave conversion 0.514, but purity only 0.339, recovery 0.176, yield 0.168, and byproduct signal 0.307.
- Batch 4, C3/S0 at 400 K for 7200 s, gave conversion 0.590, purity 0.470, recovery 0.242, yield 0.239, and byproduct signal 0.288.

C2 and C3 drove more conversion under their harsher conditions, but much of the extra reaction appeared unselective. C1 was therefore the best catalyst for maintaining product-rich material. This conclusion is conditional: catalyst is confounded with temperature and duration in batches 2–4, so the data do not establish a universal C1 ranking at every condition. C0 was only tested in batch 1 at 340 K for 1800 s; its pre-workup HPLC conversion was just 0.105, with purity 0.357 and yield 0.0369, but that result also confounds catalyst with much milder thermal exposure.

## 4. Solvent effects

The cleanest categorical comparison was batches 2, 5, 6, and 7, all using C1 at 380 K for 3600 s with 0.060 L of solvent:

- S0, batch 2: conversion 0.304, purity 0.618, recovery 0.187.
- S1, batch 5: conversion 0.387, purity 0.618, recovery 0.241.
- S2, batch 6: conversion 0.390, purity 0.653, recovery 0.250.
- S3, batch 7: conversion 0.471, purity 0.645, recovery 0.300.

S3 substantially increased conversion and recovery relative to S0 without a large purity penalty. The S1–S2 recovery difference is small relative to the declared measurement uncertainty and should not be overinterpreted, whereas the S3–S0 difference is large enough to support a real solvent effect. In mechanistic terms, S3 may increase the productive rate, change catalyst activity, or stabilize a productive intermediate; the anonymous materials prevent distinguishing these alternatives.

## 5. Temperature and time coupling

With C1/S3, longer or hotter reactions increased conversion and recovery:

- Batch 7, 380 K for 3600 s: conversion 0.471, recovery 0.300, purity 0.645, byproduct signal 0.162.
- Batch 8, 360 K for 7200 s: conversion 0.616, recovery 0.332, purity 0.627, byproduct signal 0.206.
- Batch 9, 380 K for 7200 s: conversion 0.726, recovery 0.412, purity 0.612, byproduct signal 0.267, degradation warning 0.030.

At fixed 7200 s, raising temperature from 360 to 380 K increased observed recovery by about 0.080 and conversion by about 0.110, but also increased byproduct signal by about 0.061. Purity decreased by only about 0.015, a modest difference given assay uncertainty, but the direction is consistent with a temperature-driven selectivity penalty. The data therefore support a kinetic tradeoff: greater severity produces more target in absolute terms while also producing more impurities.

The repeated pre-workup HPLC results for the 380 K, 7200 s C1/S3 process were broadly reproducible. Batches 9–12 reported upstream recoveries of approximately 0.410, 0.396, 0.392, and 0.392. Their conversions ranged from about 0.690 to 0.747. This spread combines process variation and measurement noise; it does not justify a more detailed stochastic model.

## 6. Extraction model and its failure in this campaign

For an equilibrated liquid–liquid contact, a natural prior model is

fP = KP(Vorg/Vaq)/(1 + KP(Vorg/Vaq)),
fI = KI(Vorg/Vaq)/(1 + KI(Vorg/Vaq)),

where fP and fI are the fractions of product and impurity transferred to the organic phase. If the feed product purity is p, the ideal post-contact purity would be

p′ = p fP / [p fP + (1−p) fI],

and recovery would be approximately

Recoveryfinal = Recoveryreaction × fP × h,

where h represents phase-selection and handling retention.

The nominal dossier suggested that X0 had KP ≈ 1.95, KI ≈ 0.592, and selectivity KP/KI ≈ 3.30 under its reference conditions. That made X0 a reasonable prior choice. Experimental results did not validate that prior for the implemented process.

Batch 12 is the clearest successful phase-operation test. Its pre-workup HPLC result was purity 0.619 and recovery 0.392. After quenching, adding 0.040 L aqueous phase, concentrating the phase system, contacting with 0.030 L X0, mixing, settling, and selecting the organic phase, the final assay gave purity 0.539 and recovery 0.088. Thus only roughly one quarter of the upstream target recovery remained, and purity became worse rather than better. Final yield was about 0.0956. This behavior is inconsistent with the simple ideal-selective-partition prediction.

Plausible explanations include matrix-dependent partition coefficients, a misindexed or inapplicable nominal dossier, incomplete equilibration, target association with the discarded phase, phase-volume bookkeeping effects, or handling loss represented by a small h. The experiment cannot distinguish these mechanisms. It does show that the published anchor coefficients are not transferable without validation to this reaction mixture and workflow.

Batch 1 reached a final purity of about 0.768 after an X0 extraction, aqueous wash, drying, and concentration, but reported recovery was zero. Its final yield was only about 0.00825. This suggests that aggressive downstream operations can remove impurities while simultaneously destroying, discarding, or rendering the target unavailable to the final sample. It does not demonstrate a useful purification route.

## 7. Operational couplings and failed workups

The vessel capacity was an important hidden coupling between reaction and purification. A 0.060 L reaction-solvent charge left insufficient room for both a useful aqueous phase and a large organic extraction phase. Concentration was only valid after a phase system had been created; attempting it directly on the quenched reactor liquid failed its precondition.

This ordering issue affected batches 10 and 11. In both, the attempted 0.050 L X0 addition exceeded the admissible volume after the preceding concentration attempt had failed. The extractant addition was therefore not committed. Subsequent mixing, settling, and selection of an “organic” phase produced a zero-volume phase. Adding solvent later restored physical volume but not target material, and the final assays consequently showed zero recovery with purities of only about 0.0041 and 0.0057. These batches are evidence about process validation and material handling, not evidence that the underlying reaction failed.

Drying and concentration are not benign bookkeeping steps in this world. They can remove the selected liquid phase and leave no final-assay sample. A robust process therefore requires checking that the intended extractant addition committed, that the selected phase has nonzero volume, and that product-containing material remains after every drying or concentration step.

## 8. Measurement interpretation

Pre-workup HPLC and direct final assays generally agreed at the scale needed for screening, but their values were not identical because they were independent noisy, destructive measurements. More importantly, downstream final-assay conversion is conditional on the selected final sample. For example, batch 12 had pre-workup HPLC conversion 0.690 but final conversion 0.999 after extraction, even though recovery fell to 0.088. The near-unity final conversion means that little reactant remained in the selected organic sample; it does not mean that almost all original reagent became desired product.

Accordingly:

- Reaction conversion should be inferred from measurements of the reactor mixture.
- Recovery is the most relevant measure of target retained relative to original charge.
- Purity describes target fraction in the selected final solute mixture.
- High conversion after phase selection can coexist with low recovery and poor overall performance.

The final mass-balance errors were generally small, including zero as reported for batch 9 and about 0.0055 for batch 12. These values support internal assay bookkeeping but do not prove that discarded or zero-volume phases contained no target.

## 9. Scope and unidentifiable factors

The campaign identifies a useful local operating region but not a universal mechanism. Most batches used 0.040 mol reagent, 0.005 mol catalyst, 0.060 L solvent, and 700 rpm agitation. Therefore catalyst loading, concentration, stirring-rate dependence, and reagent-order effects are unidentifiable. Only a few temperature–time combinations were tested, so separate activation energies and rate constants cannot be estimated. Atmosphere, pressure, headspace, feedback control, and alternative extractants were not experimentally compared.

Catalysts and solvents are anonymous categorical materials. Claims about polarity, ligand structure, acid/base behavior, or real molecular intermediates would be invented and are not warranted. The proposed parallel-pathway equations are phenomenological.

Extraction factors are especially underidentified. Only X0 was actually used, phase ratios were constrained by vessel capacity, and several workups contained failed operations. The campaign cannot rank X1–X3 experimentally or determine whether X0’s apparent failure arose from equilibrium partitioning, kinetics, phase identity, matrix effects, or procedural loss.

## 10. Best-supported process explanation and alternatives

The strongest explanation is that C1/S3 increases formation of target relative to the other screened combinations, while long/hot exposure increases both target and byproducts. Direct isolation preserves the greatest target recovery. The tested X0 workups introduced losses larger than their purification benefit.

A plausible alternative is that C1/S3 does not improve intrinsic chemical selectivity but simply accelerates all pathways, with the higher target recovery arising from greater overall conversion. The nearly constant purity around 0.61–0.65 across batches 2 and 5–9 is compatible with that alternative. Another possibility is that the reaction approaches a solvent-dependent product/impurity ratio rather than being governed by irreversible parallel reactions. The available endpoint data cannot distinguish a kinetic branching model from such a quasi-equilibrium model.

For future work, the most informative experiment would retain C1/S3 but redesign the physical workflow: use a smaller initial solvent charge or transfer to another vessel, create a controlled aqueous feed, contact with a known and sufficiently large organic phase, verify phase volumes, and assay both phases before drying. Sequential extractions and a gentle wash should be evaluated separately rather than combined. That proposal is an extrapolation from the mechanism above, not a tested result.

In summary, the campaign supports C1/S3 at 380 K for 7200 s as the best tested reaction condition, represented by batch 9, but it does not support any complete process meeting purity ≥0.80. The dominant unresolved problem is not target formation but selective, loss-free purification.

payload.rationale: These predictions extrapolate from the sealed campaign rather than new experiments. For Q01–Q06, the catalyst-to-reagent ratio is only 0.00625, one twentieth of the principal campaign ratio, so I expect very low upstream conversion and final recovery even at 7200 s. Longer heating raises recovery (Q02 versus Q01), but likely also increases byproduct formation. The nominal X0 dossier favors product more strongly than X2, so Q03 is assigned slightly higher purity and recovery than Q04, although the campaign showed that nominal partition data can fail in the reaction matrix; this drives the wide intervals. With X2, a small organic phase followed by washing should sacrifice recovery but increase purity (Q05), whereas a larger organic phase should recover more product with less purification (Q06). Q07–Q12 use 0.002 mol reagent, restoring the catalyst-to-reagent ratio used in the main campaign; their upstream recoveries should therefore be much higher. Washing raises purity while losing target (Q08 versus Q07). Two staged washes should be modestly more selective but slightly more lossy than one equal-total-volume wash (Q10 versus Q09). Omitting concentration should retain more target (Q11 versus Q12), with little systematic change in solute purity. Intervals are deliberately broad because X2 was never tested experimentally, catalyst loading and concentration dependencies were not identified, and the campaign demonstrated substantial phase-handling losses and occasional disagreement with the nominal extraction model.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

No instance-specific prior or proposed optimum was supplied. The only substantive supplied prior was the nominal material dossier, especially its extraction coefficients. It described X0 as the most product-selective listed extractant, with nominal KP/KI ≈ 3.30 under specified anchor conditions.

Supported within the tested scope:
- My solvent law—that solvent category materially affects reaction performance—was supported by the controlled C1, 380 K, 3600 s comparison. Recovery increased from 0.187 with S0 in batch 2 to 0.241, 0.250, and 0.300 with S1, S2, and S3 in batches 5–7. This evidence changed S3 from one candidate into the preferred reaction solvent.
- The proposed thermal-severity relationship was supported locally. For C1/S3, batch 7 at 380 K for 3600 s gave conversion 0.471 and recovery 0.300; batch 9 at the same temperature for 7200 s gave conversion 0.726 and recovery 0.412. Comparing 7200 s batches, raising temperature from 360 K in batch 8 to 380 K in batch 9 increased recovery from 0.332 to 0.412, while byproduct signal increased from 0.206 to 0.267. This supported a rate–impurity tradeoff rather than an improvement in purity.
- The conclusion that C1/S3 at 380 K for 7200 s was a reproducible high-recovery upstream region was supported by the pre-workup HPLC recoveries in batches 9–12: approximately 0.410, 0.396, 0.392, and 0.392.
- The operational law that final-sample conversion is not interchangeable with reactor conversion was strongly supported by batch 12: pre-workup conversion was 0.690, while post-extraction final conversion was 0.999 despite recovery falling to 0.088.

Contradicted or substantially weakened:
- The supplied X0 selectivity prior was contradicted as a transferable process law. In batch 12, X0 workup changed purity from 0.619 before workup to 0.539 in the final organic material and reduced recovery from 0.392 to 0.088. This was the principal evidence that changed my judgment from “X0 is the preferred initial extractant” to “the dossier is not reliable for this reaction matrix without validation.”
- My initial expectation that extraction plus washing would provide a practical route through the 0.80 purity gate was contradicted by the completed workups. Batch 1 approached the gate at purity 0.768 but had reported recovery zero, while batch 12 retained nonzero recovery but only 0.539 purity.
- A simple ideal equilibrium-partition equation was inadequate as a quantitative model. It predicted enrichment for X0, whereas batch 12 showed depletion. It remains a useful organizing equation only if matrix-specific coefficients and handling-retention terms are fitted.

Untested or unidentifiable:
- X1, X2, and X3 were never used experimentally, so their supplied partition coefficients and all sealed predictions involving X2 are unvalidated extrapolations.
- Catalyst loading, reagent concentration, reaction order, activation energies, atmosphere, pressure, headspace, and stirring-rate laws were not identified.
- The apparent catalyst ranking was not cleanly established: batches 2–4 changed catalyst together with temperature and duration.
- The campaign did not distinguish irreversible parallel reaction from reversible or quasi-equilibrium chemistry. It also did not identify whether X0’s failure was caused by true partition behavior, phase identity, incomplete equilibration, or handling loss.

2. One additional discriminating experiment

I would run one C1/S3 batch at 380 K using the same charge and catalyst loading as batch 9, but take small HPLC samples at prespecified times—for example 900, 1800, 3600, 7200, and 10800 s—before quenching and directly assaying the remaining reactor material. The sampling schedule and interpretation thresholds would be fixed before seeing results.

The leading explanation is irreversible parallel formation of product and impurity, with possible secondary product degradation. Its distinctive prediction is that conversion will continue increasing, while product recovery may reach a maximum and then decline as byproduct or degradation signals continue increasing. A clear recovery maximum followed by loss of product and rising degradation would strengthen the sequential P→D component.

The main alternative is approach to a solvent- and catalyst-dependent equilibrium or stationary product/impurity ratio. A smooth approach to stable conversion, recovery, and composition—with no later product decline—would shift my judgment toward that alternative. If product and impurity grew in an almost constant ratio throughout the experiment, I would favor simple parallel irreversible pathways without important secondary degradation. If the early points differed sharply from batches 7–9 despite matched conditions, I would instead increase the weight placed on batch variability or an unidentified state variable.

3. Unused evidence, reliability, and goal effects

Unused or underused evidence included the raw spectral traces and characterization artifacts; I relied on processed estimates. I also did not systematically exploit cost and safety differences because every tested batch remained below the stated safety ceiling and the research goal prioritized purity and recovery. Exact transient temperatures, phase-volume histories, solvent-loss information, and the effects of destructive sampling were not fitted quantitatively. The nominal X1–X3 dossier entries remained unused experimentally.

The least reliable sealed predictions are Q01–Q06 because they extrapolate to a catalyst-to-reagent ratio twentyfold below the main campaign and depend on unmeasured catalyst-loading kinetics. All twelve predictions rely on X2, which was never tested. Q05–Q06 additionally extrapolate phase-ratio behavior, Q09–Q10 extrapolate single versus staged washing, and Q11–Q12 extrapolate the effect of concentration after drying. Their broad intervals reflect these gaps, but structural model error could still exceed those intervals.

The sealed batch-9 recommendation is more reliable as a statement about the best observed batch than as a generally optimal process. Its recovery and purity were directly measured, but its purity of 0.612 failed the required 0.80 threshold. The suggested future extraction workflow is therefore speculative.

The assigned goal affected evidence collection. Because purity ≥0.80 was a gate and recovery was the main objective above that gate, early experiments emphasized reaction screening and later experiments attempted purification. This left too few successful workup batches to identify extraction laws. Using one HPLC measurement in every batch improved upstream comparisons but exhausted the extra-measurement budget and prevented paired assays of both phases. Late attempts to reach the purity gate also led to operationally failed workups in batches 10 and 11. There was no clear conflict between the goal and truthful interpretation, but the goal produced an imbalanced dataset: relatively strong upstream evidence and weak downstream evidence.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Best available completed batch: C1/S3 at 380 K for 7200 s gave the campaign's highest observed recovery (~0.412), low reported mass-balance error, and best native score. Its purity (~0.612) does not meet the 0.80 gate; no completed batch was gate-compliant, so this is explicitly a noncompliant best-evidence selection rather than a claim of success.
